title: Anthropomorphism and Divine Attributes
english: They were acting, and they were being destroyed together with the man, through whom he also came to fulfill his own needs, a life-spark being left behind with Noah and from them.

Likewise, men were also perishing as wickedness increased upon the earth, because they sinned by thinking with the evil, not casually but through careful use of sins. Let us carefully examine what was said from the beginning: 'The Lord God having seen,' he says, 'that the wickednesses of men had been multiplied upon the earth' (Gen 6:5). For did he not previously see their wickednesses? But it is evident that now he has seen them for the purpose of vengeance. For when he does not wish to send punishments to those sinning, it is said he does not see them, which is to say when he is sleeping, while others are watching. It is indeed said by someone: 'I awoke to my impieties,' and after having tested the patience of God through many impieties, after those who reproach had passed by, he says: 'I awoke to my impieties.' And another saint said: 'He arose like one sleeping, like a strong man having roared from wine'; for having been very patient, he comes excessively and unceasingly with punishments to those in such need, which is why the unceasingness and the multitude is called an awakening and a roaring from wine. For it is like a good physician to use the sufferings at the right time, which is made evident by 'The Lord God having seen.'

And if it is about to be that 'everyone thinks in his heart toward evil things' (Genesis 6:5), even though Noah did not have it so, we should not be surprised; for it is said regarding the majority in this way, just as 'every brother betrays and every friend acts deceitfully' (Prov 27:6). And it is possible, since Noah was not at all a man—for he had ascended beyond the human condition—that this was said as not being applicable to him at all among men, but happening to a god, as it is said: 'He called those gods to whom the word of God came.' Similar to this is also 'I said in my ecstasy: every man is a liar' (Ps 53:6); for he was a god, as we have demonstrated, the one saying these things. For if a man were not thus, if he were a liar, then 'every man' would no longer be true.

Not a liar, but speaking the truth, yet he is not a man himself, who is called a man through excellence beyond human measure, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy, are you not men, as these also walk?' (James 3:16). For their malice was not practiced by them by chance, but with care and deliberation; for this reveals what is in the heart (Luke 6:45).

Likewise, 'from youth' can be understood in two ways: either being smeared with evil from a small age, or that no one among those described as a man is an elder, even if the nature is so, setting forward the novelties and the instabilities. 'For old age is not an honorable thing measured by long life or by the number of years; for much is wisdom to men, and old age is a life without a cloud' (Sirach 4:10). And it is not unlikely that the 'youth of sin' and 'remember not my ignorance' (Psalm 25:11) carry interpretations saying: 'Remember not whatever evil things I have done.'

Having said these things, it is worthy to consider what is revealed from 'God remembered that he made man upon the earth' (Psalm 8:4) and 'I was grieved that I made them' (Psalm 8:5), which is equivalent to 'I repented that I made Saul king' (1 Samuel 15:11). It must be said, however, that things are said about God in a human manner, and not in the way the words and the thought possess. For if hands, feet, eyes, and ears are transferred in the Scripture, one must not think that God is formed in a human way, but it is clear that we shall call each of these things regarding the active powers of God, such as hands and the unretreating eyes, and likewise his discerning eyes and his practical hands, even if through another understanding.

For indeed, regarding sensible things, each of the named things signifies only one thing, such as wood; but regarding God, they are called by many names, which are to be understood by the word as preceding the various things about him. For so God is called both Spirit and Source, and again hands and feet are said to belong to him; yet nowhere, even if he had something sensible, were his names so many; for neither light nor Spirit nor Source have hands.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Grace, Virtue, and the Increase of Faith
english: It was thought and regretted as if regarding an unchangeable mind. For just as men, wishing to present a confession to those being taught by themselves that they erred greatly and are unworthy of lessons, say: 'I regretted that I gave so much to you, leading you to the knowledge of the transgression,' so also God is said to not undergo a passion of regret, but rather to speak for the sake of the manifestation of the greatness of the sin. For He did not not know that such things would be, but through goodness He viewed whether perhaps from the laws written according to the intellect [they would follow]. We use an image toward it not being a passion of God, but of those who change in such a way.

Let someone be wise... [gaps]... and because of this an heir... [gaps]... he himself did not change according to the mind among those changed, when the property came to the righteous alone; for this one had the purpose from the beginning. And good is 'I will blot out the man whom I have made from the face of the earth' (Genesis 6:7); for He does not lead him into non-existence, nor does He blot him out according to the soul, but from the earth. And this is not only the work of God, having been deceived by evil, to destroy men, but also through a sign to destroy the one dwelling in the earth being a lowly one; for the lowly one is a resident of the earth, the holy one being not a resident but a sojourner. Thus also it is said in Jeremiah: 'The evils shall be burned upon those dwelling on the earth' (Jer 5:31), those rooting themselves on the earth, which the holy one says he did not suffer, thanking: 'In a short time He has brought me to an end in the land' (Ps 116:7), and in the Revelation it is said: 'Woe to those dwelling on the earth' (Rev 6:10), not to those sojourning; but the purpose of God is to snatch the man from the earthlings, even if he himself holds to the earthlings.

'But Noah found grace in the sight of the Lord God' (Gen 6:8). It is great and heavenly to find grace in the sight of God, and this is accomplished through pleasing Him, which follows that to please men, the one pleasing to men not always pleasing to God. For see what the blessed Paul says: 'If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a Christ's slave' (Gal 1:10).

Then I would not have been, and the Psalmist says: 'The Lord scatters the bones of those who please men' (Ps 52:9). But those who have the grace from God say: 'He who has graced us along with the beloved' (Eph 1:6), just as Mary also hears from the angel: 'Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you' (Luke 1:28). For this is the grace, to have the Lord with oneself; and one has the Lord with oneself by being distinguished by virtue and good deeds, saying: 'If you seek the testing of the Christ speaking in me' (1 Cor 4:9).

For He himself gives grace and peace; for this is what the holy man prays for, saying: 'Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 13:13). And God gives this gift, having provided us the occasion to receive it. For it is said in Proverbs: 'Grace and friendship set free, which you have kept for yourself, so that you may not become despised' (Prov 28:14); for in the power of one's own choice is the ability to keep these and to succeed.

Thus also Noah found grace in the sight of the Lord God from his own domestic preparation, himself having graced himself through works of virtue and from this having received grace from God; for the God of all, working together with those succeeding and striving on our part, adds to, adorns, and leads into the greatness of good. The disciples of the Savior, knowing this, having already pre-succeeded in the faith toward him, were saying to him, knowing that faith is also God-given: 'Increase our faith' (Luke 17:5).

For just as a word of wisdom is given through the Spirit and a word of knowledge according to the Spirit (1 Cor 12:8), so also faith is in the same Spirit. For it is impossible to receive the faith given from God according to grace without having that which is established from our own part. For this is made clear from 'increase our faith' (Luke 22:32); but even Isaiah says, from the person of the Lord's man, or even from himself: 'He has added to me an ear for hearing, and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Isa 50:4); for the hearing and instruction given toward God opens even these ears to hear the intellect more divinely.

Thus also let us understand 'grace for grace' (John 1:16), understanding the one from God approaching through our own part. And also let us understand the 'found' [which was] said, so that it might be shown that having sought...

title: Partial Perfection and Noah's Character
english: He found it rightly, those who do not seek in the way they ought, not finding; for they say, 'They shall seek me,' yet 'evil men and they shall not find' (John 14:20). From this it is known that he sought well from the judgment and gift of God, when, as if sealing the grace himself, he gives: 'Not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the merciful God' (Romans 3:27), and 'If the Lord builds a house, in vain the builders labored for it' (Psalm 127:1).

Yes, 9. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God (Genesis 6:9). The genealogy of the righteous is not so much of men as of virtues; for these are his preceding offspring. This indeed teaches the written Spirit; for it being the case to say the generations of Noah, it brought forward: 'Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God' (Genesis 6:9).

Let us see what is signified by 'perfect in his generation.' According to a first interpretation, one might say that, compared to the men of his own time who had endowed themselves with immeasurable evil, he was perfect; this is not a great thing, if he were compared to the unknown, for it might perhaps be possible to say that of those entering the ark with him, he was called perfect because he was different; for it is indeed likely that they were such from the holy habit.

It might also be said thus: the generation of the righteous is similarity, and this is signified from 'This is the generation of those seeking him' (Psalm 14:3); for having said, 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who has innocent hands and is pure in heart' (Psalm 24:3-4) and the following, he brought forward: 'This is the generation of those seeking him,' having spoken of one generation of those adorned with the same virtue. By this, in the opposite way, similarly, it is the thing said: 'Sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation'; for the generation of such things is the similar state and way of life.

And it is necessary to hear 'perfect' as it is in men, which Paul said to know perfectly in part, saying concerning the perfect: 'When the perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away' (1 Corinthians 13:10); all the perfection being accomplished in men is as towards that in the future.

An age is complete only in part. Let what is said be clear by way of an example: he who is in the first letters is complete, yet as far as the one listening to grammatical discourse, he is incomplete. And the Apostle himself, saying, 'We know in part and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor 13:9), speaks this concerning himself and those like him: 'As for those who are perfect, we think this,' and 'But we speak wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 1:6); for just as the citizenship existing there is incomplete, as we have said, as far as the knowledge that is to come, being 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12), even if it has reached its utmost limit.

And the things said about Noah—that he was righteous, and perfect, and pleasing to God—must be taken all at once, even if the words have an order; for he was 'righteous' and 'being perfect' he had a pleasingness toward God. But the perfect and the righteous are anticipated by the pleasingness; for it is not that because he pleased, he became righteous and perfect, but because he appeared righteous and perfect, he has been shown to be pleasing to God. And if Noah is said to be a man of such a state, it is not necessary to be surprised, since we have often observed that the name 'man' signifies more; for it is not regarding mere dust alone, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not acting as men and walking according to man?' (1 Corinthians 3:3), and concerning the devil sowing evil thoughts, it is said: 'A man has done this' (John 6:70); here, in addition to declaring the nature, it also signifies the 'man' as the one who saves according to the 'image' (Gen 1:26). And also, that he 'being perfect pleased God' (Genesis 6:9); for he pleased God having already been promised perfection, not pleasing God by pleasing in everything, but by being [pleasing] to both righteous men and in other ways to men; for he is praised not only for pleasing the righteous, but after [that] for pleasing God.

10. And Noah fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. He fathered three sons, and Noah became a father of such a number; for nothing was said before this of having had another child. The explicit part is clear; but if one looks toward an upward leading, he might say that one fathering two of a certain physical sex would be casting symbols; for the two are kindred in matter, for this is divisible; but the one who fathered three is called perfect, being first to bear a complete image.
